skills.title: Basic French Phrases
skills.description: Greetings and polite phrases for travel and chat.

lessons.title: Greetings in French
lessons.content:
Bonjour means hello or good day. Use Bonsoir in the evening. To say goodbye, use Au revoir. To be polite, say S'il vous plaît for please and Merci for thank you.

To ask how someone is, say Comment allez-vous? A friendly answer is Très bien, merci.

questions.text: What does 'Merci' mean?
Which phrase means goodbye?

skills.title: Japanese Hiragana Basics
skills.description: Read and write the first Japanese characters.

lessons.title: What is Hiragana?
lessons.content:
Hiragana is one of the Japanese writing systems. Each character stands for a sound, such as あ (a), い (i), う (u), え (e) and お (o).

These five are the vowels. Almost every other hiragana sound is a consonant plus one of these vowels, for example か is ka and き is ki.

questions.text: Which of these is a Japanese vowel sound?
What does each hiragana character represent?

skills.title: English Grammar Basics
skills.description: Sentences, nouns, verbs and simple tenses.

lessons.title: Nouns and Verbs
lessons.content:
A noun names a person, place or thing, like teacher, city or book. A verb shows an action or a state, like run, write or is.

Every complete sentence needs at least a subject (the noun doing something) and a verb. In 'Ana reads', Ana is the subject and reads is the verb.

questions.text: Which word is a verb?
In 'Ana reads', which word is the subject?

skills.title: JavaScript Basics
skills.description: The language of the web, from variables to functions.

lessons.title: Variables and Data Types
lessons.content:
A variable is a named box that stores a value, such as age = 21 or name = "Ana". The value can change while the program runs.

Common data types are numbers, strings (text) and booleans (true or false). Choosing the right type matters, because you cannot do math on text.

questions.text: Which data type stores the text "Ana"?
What does a variable do?
options: Stores a value under a name

skills.title: HTML & CSS Basics
skills.description: Build and style your first web page.

lessons.title: Your First Web Page
lessons.content:
HTML describes the content of a page using tags, such as

for a heading and

for a paragraph. Tags usually come in pairs: an opening tag and a closing tag. CSS controls how the page looks, such as colors, spacing and fonts. For example, color: blue; makes text blue.

questions.text: Which language controls how a page looks?
Which tag makes a heading?

skills.title: SQL Basics
skills.description: Ask questions of a database.

lessons.title: Selecting Data
lessons.content:
SQL is the language used to talk to databases. A database stores data in tables made of rows and columns.

To read data you use SELECT. For example, SELECT name FROM users; returns the name column for every row in the users table. Add WHERE to filter rows.

questions.text: Which command reads data from a table?
Which word filters the rows you get back?

skills.title: Color Theory
skills.description: Choose colors that look good together.

lessons.title: The Basics of Color
lessons.content:
Color has three parts: hue (the color itself), saturation (how strong it is) and brightness (how light or dark).

Colors opposite each other on the color wheel, like blue and orange, are complementary and make each other stand out. Colors next to each other, like blue and green, are analogous and feel calm together.

questions.text: Which pair is complementary?
What does saturation describe?
options: How strong or vivid the color is

skills.title: Typography Basics
skills.description: Pick and pair fonts for readable designs.

lessons.title: Serif and Sans-serif
lessons.content:
Serif fonts have small strokes at the ends of letters, like Times New Roman. Sans-serif fonts do not, like Arial.

For good design, use no more than two or three fonts. Make headings larger and bolder than body text, and leave enough space between lines so text is easy to read.

questions.text: Which kind of font has small strokes at the ends of letters?
About how many fonts should one design use?

skills.title: Logo Design Basics
skills.description: Make simple, memorable logos.

lessons.title: What Makes a Good Logo
lessons.content:
A good logo is simple, memorable and works at any size, from a tiny app icon to a large sign.

It should also work in one color, so it still looks good in black and white. Avoid too many details, because they disappear when the logo is small.

questions.text: A good logo should be...
Why should a logo work in one color?
options: It is cheaper to print everywhere and stays clear

skills.title: Music Theory Basics
skills.description: Beats, notes and how music is written.

lessons.title: Reading Beats and Rhythm
lessons.content:
Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds in music. A beat is the steady pulse you tap your foot to.

Most songs group beats into bars of four (4/4 time): count 1-2-3-4, 1-2-3-4. A quarter note lasts one beat, a half note lasts two beats and a whole note lasts four beats.

questions.text: How many beats does a half note last?
In 4/4 time, how many beats are in one bar?

skills.title: Ukulele Basics
skills.description: Play your first songs on four strings.

lessons.title: Holding and Tuning
lessons.content:
The ukulele has four strings. From the string closest to your face down, the standard tuning is G, C, E, A.

Hold the ukulele close to your body with your picking arm over the body. Press the strings with your fingertips, just behind the metal fret, for a clear sound.

questions.text: How many strings does a ukulele have?
Where should you press the string?
options: In the middle of the fret

skills.title: Singing Basics
skills.description: Breathing and posture for a stronger voice.

lessons.title: Breathing and Posture
lessons.content:
Good singing starts with good breathing. Stand with your feet apart and shoulders relaxed. Breathe in low, so your belly expands, instead of lifting your shoulders.

Breathe out slowly while you sing. Drink water and warm up with gentle humming before singing loudly.

questions.text: Where should you breathe from when singing?
What is a good warm-up?

skills.title: Smartphone Photography
skills.description: Better photos with the phone you already have.

lessons.title: The Rule of Thirds
lessons.content:
Imagine your photo split into a 3 x 3 grid with two lines across and two lines down. Place your subject where the lines cross, instead of in the exact center.

This makes the picture feel balanced and more interesting. Also leave a little space in the direction your subject is looking or moving.

questions.text: Where should you place the main subject in the rule of thirds?
How many lines does the grid use?

skills.title: Video Editing Basics
skills.description: Cut clips into a clear, watchable video.

lessons.title: Cuts and Timeline
lessons.content:
Video editing happens on a timeline, where clips are placed in order. A cut is where one clip ends and the next begins.

Keep cuts purposeful: remove pauses and mistakes, and let each clip show something new. Add music quietly so it does not cover people speaking.

questions.text: What is a cut?
options: Where one clip ends and the next begins

questions.text: How should music sound under speech?
options: Quiet enough to hear the voice

skills.title: Lighting Basics
skills.description: Use natural and simple light well.

lessons.title: Natural Light
lessons.content:
Soft light makes people look natural. The best natural light is near a window, or outdoors in the early morning or late afternoon.

Avoid harsh midday sun directly overhead, which makes strong shadows under the eyes. Face your subject toward the light, not away from it.

questions.text: When is natural light usually softest outdoors?
Which way should the subject face?

skills.title: Knitting Basics
skills.description: Cast on, knit and finish your first scarf.

lessons.title: Casting On
lessons.content:
Casting on puts your first row of stitches on the needle. Make a slip knot, place it on the needle, then pull a loop of yarn through it to add each new stitch.

Keep the stitches snug but not tight. If they are too tight you will not be able to slide the needle into them on the next row.

questions.text: What does casting on do?
options: Makes the first row of stitches

questions.text: Why shouldn't cast-on stitches be too tight?
options: You cannot slide the needle in next row

skills.title: Drawing Basics
skills.description: Lines, shapes and shading for beginners.

lessons.title: Shapes and Shading
lessons.content:
Everything can be drawn from simple shapes: circles, squares and triangles. Start with light lines, then add details.

To add shading, decide where the light comes from. Areas facing away from the light are darker. Press harder with the pencil for dark areas and lighter for bright areas.

questions.text: How should you start a drawing?
options: With simple shapes and light lines

questions.text: Which areas are darker when shading?

skills.title: Watercolor Painting Basics
skills.description: Washes, blending and color control.

lessons.title: Wet-on-Wet
lessons.content:
Watercolor uses water to spread pigment. In the wet-on-wet technique you wet the paper first, then add paint, so colors blend softly.

Use more water for light colors and less water for strong ones. Let a layer dry before adding sharp details on top.

questions.text: What do you do first in wet-on-wet?
How do you get a lighter color?

skills.title: Hip-Hop Dance Basics
skills.description: Groove, bounce and rhythm for beginners.

lessons.title: Finding the Rhythm: The Basic Step
lessons.content:
Start by standing tall with your knees soft. Listen for the beat and step on every beat: right, left, right, left.

Once you can step in time, add a small sway of the hips and let your arms move naturally. Keeping the beat matters more than fancy moves.

questions.text: What should you do first when learning a basic step?
options: Step in time with the beat

questions.text: Which matters more for a beginner?

skills.title: Ballroom Dance Basics
skills.description: Posture and the basic box step.

lessons.title: Posture and the Box Step
lessons.content:
Ballroom dancing starts with good posture: stand tall, shoulders relaxed and chest lifted. Hold your partner in a gentle frame, not stiff.

The basic box step moves in a square: step forward, step to the side, close your feet together, then repeat backward. Count the steps out loud to stay in time.

questions.text: What shape does the basic box step follow?
How should you hold your posture?

skills.title: Folk Dance Basics
skills.description: Group steps and traditional rhythms.

lessons.title: Dancing in a Group
lessons.content:
Many folk dances are done in lines, circles or pairs. The pattern repeats, so learn one short section first.

Watch the leader, listen to the music and keep a steady step. Smiling and staying in time with the group matters more than doing every step perfectly.

questions.text: How should you learn a folk dance?
options: One short section at a time

questions.text: What matters in group dances?
options: Staying in time with the group

skills.title: Creative Writing Basics
skills.description: Characters, plot and voice.

lessons.title: The Shape of a Story
lessons.content:
Most stories have a beginning, a middle and an end. The beginning introduces a character and a problem. The middle shows the character trying to solve it and facing obstacles.

The end shows how the problem is resolved and how the character has changed. Even a very short story works better when something is at stake.

questions.text: What does the beginning of a story usually introduce?
What happens in the middle?

skills.title: Essay Writing Basics
skills.description: Plan and write clear essays.

lessons.title: Introduction, Body, Conclusion
lessons.content:
An essay has three parts. The introduction presents your main idea, called the thesis. The body paragraphs each cover one point with examples. The conclusion sums up your ideas.

Before writing, make a short outline so each paragraph has a clear job.

questions.text: Where does the thesis usually go?
What does each body paragraph cover?

skills.title: Journaling Basics
skills.description: Build a simple writing habit.

lessons.title: Starting a Journal
lessons.content:
Journaling means writing regularly about your thoughts, goals or day. It does not need to be perfect or long.

Pick a time that fits your routine, like before bed, and write for five minutes. If you do not know what to write, try 'Today I felt...' or 'One good thing today was...'

questions.text: How long can a journaling session be?
Does journaling need to be perfect?

skills.title: Outfit Styling Basics
skills.description: Mix and match clothes with confidence.

lessons.title: Matching Colors in an Outfit
lessons.content:
Start with one or two neutral colors such as black, white, grey, beige or navy. They go with almost everything.

Add one color as an accent, like a red scarf or green shoes. A simple rule: wear no more than three main colors in one outfit so the look stays clean.

questions.text: Which of these is a neutral color?
About how many main colors keep an outfit clean?

skills.title: Skincare Basics
skills.description: A simple daily routine for healthy skin.

lessons.title: The Simple Routine
lessons.content:
A basic skincare routine has three steps: cleanse, moisturize and protect. Wash your face gently in the morning and evening.

Use a moisturizer suited to your skin, and apply sunscreen every morning, even on cloudy days, to protect against sun damage.

questions.text: What are the three basic steps?
When should you use sunscreen?

skills.title: Basic Sewing
skills.description: Hand stitches and simple repairs.

lessons.title: Threading and the Running Stitch
lessons.content:
To sew by hand, cut a piece of thread about as long as your arm, thread the needle and tie a knot at the end.

The running stitch is the simplest: push the needle up and down through the fabric in a straight line, keeping the stitches an equal length. It is great for simple repairs.

questions.text: What is the simplest hand stitch?
What should you do at the end of the thread?

skills.title: Kitchen Basics
skills.description: Safety, knife skills and basic techniques.

lessons.title: Kitchen Safety and Knife Basics
lessons.content:
Always wash your hands before cooking and keep raw meat away from vegetables to avoid cross-contamination.

When cutting, curl your fingertips under, like a claw, and let the flat side of the knife guide against your knuckles. Use a damp towel under the cutting board so it does not slip. A sharp knife is safer than a dull one.

questions.text: Why curl your fingertips when cutting?
options: To protect your fingertips from the blade

questions.text: Which is safer?
options: A knife held by the blade

skills.title: Baking Bread Basics
skills.description: Simple dough, rising and baking.

lessons.title: Why Dough Rises
lessons.content:
Bread dough rises because yeast eats sugar and releases gas, which makes bubbles in the dough. Kneading builds gluten, which traps the gas.

Let the dough rest in a warm place until it doubles in size. Bake in a hot oven until the crust is golden and the loaf sounds hollow when tapped.

questions.text: What makes dough rise?
How do you know the dough is ready to bake?

skills.title: Healthy Meal Prep
skills.description: Plan and cook meals for the week.

lessons.title: Planning Your Week
lessons.content:
Meal prep means cooking parts of your meals ahead of time. Choose a protein, a grain and a vegetable, and cook enough for several days.

Store food in clean, covered containers in the fridge. Most cooked meals keep well for three to four days, so freeze extra portions.

questions.text: What does a balanced prepped meal include?
About how long do cooked meals keep in the fridge?

skills.title: DIY Basics
skills.description: Measuring and basic tools for home projects.

lessons.title: Using a Tape Measure and Level
lessons.content:
Measure twice, cut once. Hook the end of the tape measure on the edge of the material and read the number at the line you want.

A level shows if something is straight. When the bubble sits between the two lines in the middle, the surface is level. Use it before drilling holes for shelves or hanging frames.

questions.text: What does it mean when the bubble sits between the middle lines?
What does 'measure twice, cut once' teach?

skills.title: Basic Plumbing Fixes
skills.description: Fix leaks and clogs safely.

lessons.title: Fixing a Dripping Faucet
lessons.content:
Before any repair, turn off the water supply under the sink. A dripping faucet is often caused by a worn washer or cartridge inside.

Unscrew the handle, replace the worn part with a matching one and reassemble. Turn the water back on slowly and check for leaks.

questions.text: What should you do first before a plumbing repair?
What commonly causes a dripping faucet?

skills.title: Painting a Room
skills.description: Prepare, paint and clean up.

lessons.title: Preparing to Paint
lessons.content:
Good painting starts with preparation. Move or cover furniture, and cover the floor with a drop cloth. Fill small holes and sand rough spots.

Use painter's tape along edges. Paint the edges first with a small brush, then use a roller for large areas, working in sections.

questions.text: What do you cover the floor with?
What do you paint first?

skills.title: Home Gardening Basics
skills.description: Light, water and soil for healthy plants.

lessons.title: Watering and Sunlight
lessons.content:
Most plants need light, water and good soil. Check the label to see if a plant likes full sun, partial shade or shade.

Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, and water slowly at the base, not the leaves. Too much water is a common beginner mistake because roots need air too.

questions.text: When should you water most plants?
options: When the top inch of soil feels dry

questions.text: Where should you pour the water?
options: At the base of the plant

skills.title: Growing Herbs
skills.description: Basil, mint and herbs for the kitchen.

lessons.title: Starting Herbs at Home
lessons.content:
Herbs like basil, mint and parsley grow well in small pots on a sunny windowsill. They need about six hours of light a day.

Use pots with drainage holes. Pick leaves often, because trimming makes the plant grow bushier. Mint spreads fast, so grow it in its own pot.

questions.text: Why use pots with drainage holes?
Why grow mint in its own pot?

skills.title: Composting Basics
skills.description: Turn kitchen scraps into rich soil.

lessons.title: What to Compost
lessons.content:
Compost is made from rotting plant material. Add 'greens' like vegetable scraps and coffee grounds, and 'browns' like dry leaves and paper.

Do not add meat, dairy or oily food, because they attract pests and smell. Turn the pile now and then so air reaches it, and it will become dark, crumbly soil in a few months.

questions.text: Which is a 'green' compost item?
What should NOT go in compost?

skills.title: Car Maintenance Basics
skills.description: Simple checks that keep a car running well.

lessons.title: Checking Tire Pressure
lessons.content:
Correct tire pressure keeps the car safe, saves fuel and makes tires last longer. Find the recommended pressure on the sticker inside the driver's door.

Check pressure when the tires are cold, before driving. Unscrew the valve cap, press the gauge on the valve, read the number, then add or release air as needed.

questions.text: Where do you find the recommended pressure?
options: On a sticker inside the driver's door

questions.text: When should you check pressure?

skills.title: Motorcycle Safety Basics
skills.description: Gear and habits for safer riding.

lessons.title: Gear Up
lessons.content:
Always wear a helmet that fits well and is fastened. Add gloves, a jacket with protection, long pants and closed shoes or boots.

Before every ride, check tires, brakes, lights and mirrors. Ride at a safe speed, keep your distance and assume other drivers may not see you.

questions.text: What is the most important piece of gear?
What should you check before every ride?

skills.title: Changing a Flat Tire
skills.description: Step-by-step spare tire change.

lessons.title: Before You Lift the Car
lessons.content:
Park on flat, firm ground, turn on your hazard lights and apply the parking brake. Find the spare tire, jack and wrench in the trunk.

Loosen the wheel nuts slightly while the tire is still on the ground. Then lift the car with the jack, remove the nuts and swap the tire. Tighten the nuts in a star pattern.

questions.text: Where should you park to change a tire?
options: In the middle of the road

questions.text: When should you loosen the wheel nuts?
options: After the car is fully in the air

skills.title: Study Skills
skills.description: Habits that make studying work.

lessons.title: Study Habits That Work
lessons.content:
Short, regular study sessions beat one long late-night session. Study for 25 minutes, then rest for 5 minutes. This is called the Pomodoro technique.

Test yourself instead of only rereading. Closing the book and trying to recall what you learned helps memory more than highlighting.

questions.text: What does the Pomodoro technique suggest?
Which helps memory more?

skills.title: Algebra Basics
skills.description: Solve simple equations step by step.

lessons.title: Solving for x
lessons.content:
An equation says two things are equal. To solve for x, do the same thing to both sides so the equation stays balanced.

For example, in x + 3 = 10, subtract 3 from both sides to get x = 7. Always check your answer by putting it back in the equation.

questions.text: In x + 3 = 10, what is x?
What must you do to keep an equation balanced?
options: Do the same to both sides

skills.title: Reading Comprehension
skills.description: Understand and remember what you read.

lessons.title: Finding the Main Idea
lessons.content:
The main idea is what a text is mostly about. Often it appears in the first or last sentence of a paragraph.

While reading, ask yourself: Who or what is this about, and what is the author saying about it? Then try to say it in one sentence of your own words.

questions.text: What is the main idea?
options: What the text is mostly about

questions.text: A good way to check you understood is to...
options: Say it in your own words

skills.title: Fractions & Percentages
skills.description: Parts of a whole, in everyday numbers.

lessons.title: Fractions and Percentages
lessons.content:
A fraction shows part of a whole: 1/2 means one of two equal parts. To turn a fraction into a percentage, divide the top by the bottom and multiply by 100, so 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%.

To find a percentage of a number, multiply. For example, 10% of 200 is 0.10 x 200 = 20.

questions.text: What is 1/2 as a percentage?
What is 10% of 200?

skills.title: Physics: Motion Basics
skills.description: Speed, distance and time.

lessons.title: Speed, Distance and Time
lessons.content:
Speed tells how fast something moves. The formula is speed = distance divided by time.

If a car travels 120 kilometers in 2 hours, its speed is 120 / 2 = 60 kilometers per hour. You can also find distance by multiplying speed by time.

questions.text: If a car travels 120 km in 2 hours, what is its speed?
What is the speed formula?

skills.title: Chemistry Basics
skills.description: Atoms, elements and the periodic table.

lessons.title: Atoms and Elements
lessons.content:
Everything is made of tiny particles called atoms. An element is a type of atom, such as hydrogen, oxygen or carbon.

The periodic table organizes all known elements. Atoms join together to form molecules, for example two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom make a water molecule, H2O.

questions.text: What is H2O?
What are things made of?

skills.title: Personal Budgeting
skills.description: Plan your money with simple rules.

lessons.title: Needs, Wants and Savings
lessons.content:
A budget is a plan for your money. Write down your income, then split spending into needs (rent, food, transport), wants (eating out, games) and savings.

A simple starting rule is 50% needs, 30% wants and 20% savings. Adjust the numbers to fit your life, but always pay yourself first by saving before you spend.

questions.text: Which is a need?
In the 50/30/20 rule, what does 20% cover?

skills.title: Starting a Small Business
skills.description: From idea to first customer.

lessons.title: Validating Your Idea
lessons.content:
Before investing a lot, check that people actually want your product. Talk to possible customers and ask what problems they have.

Start small, such as selling to a few people, and learn from their feedback. This is cheaper than building everything first and hoping it sells.

questions.text: What should you do before investing a lot?
Why start small?
options: It is cheaper and you learn from feedback

skills.title: Basic Investing
skills.description: Risk, return and starting early.

lessons.title: Risk and Return
lessons.content:
Investing means putting money into something that may grow over time. Higher possible returns usually come with higher risk, meaning you could lose money.

Spread your money across different investments, called diversification, so one bad result does not hurt everything. Only invest money you will not need soon.

questions.text: What is diversification?
What usually comes with higher returns?

skills.title: Marketing Basics
skills.description: Reach the right people with the right message.

lessons.title: Know Your Audience
lessons.content:
Marketing works best when you know who you are talking to. Describe your ideal customer: their age, interests, problems and where they spend time online.

Then choose the platform that fits them, and write content that solves a problem they have. A clear message to the right people beats a loud message to everyone.

questions.text: What should you do first in marketing?
Which is better?
options: A clear message to the right people

skills.title: Social Media Content Basics
skills.description: Plan posts people want to see.

lessons.title: Planning Content
lessons.content:
Plan your posts ahead with a content calendar. Mix helpful posts, entertaining posts and posts about your product.

Use a clear first line and a strong picture. After posting, check which posts got the most likes, comments and shares, and make more of those.

questions.text: What is a content calendar?
options: A plan of posts ahead of time

questions.text: What should you do after posting?

skills.title: Email Marketing Basics
skills.description: Write emails people open and read.

lessons.title: Writing a Good Subject Line
lessons.content:
The subject line decides whether people open your email. Keep it short, clear and honest, and say what is inside.

In the email, use one main message and one clear button or link. Always let people unsubscribe, because it is respectful and often required by law.

questions.text: What does the subject line decide?
Should people be able to unsubscribe?

skills.title: Confident Speaking
skills.description: Calm nerves and speak clearly.

lessons.title: Beating Stage Fright
lessons.content:
Nervousness before speaking is normal, and even experienced speakers feel it. Practice your talk out loud several times so the words feel familiar.

Take slow breaths before you start, speak a little slower than normal, and pause between ideas. Look at friendly faces in the audience instead of the whole crowd.

questions.text: What helps calm nerves before speaking?
How should you pace your speech?

skills.title: Presentation Slides Basics
skills.description: Make slides that help, not distract.

lessons.title: Less Text, More Clarity
lessons.content:
Slides should support what you say, not replace it. Use short phrases instead of full paragraphs, and a large, easy-to-read font.

One main idea per slide is a good rule. Use pictures or simple charts to explain, and avoid reading the slide word for word.

questions.text: How many main ideas should a slide have?
Should you read the slide word for word?

skills.title: Interview Skills
skills.description: Prepare for common interview questions.

lessons.title: Preparing Your Answers
lessons.content:
Before an interview, learn about the company and read the job description. Prepare short answers to common questions, such as 'Tell me about yourself' and 'Why do you want this job?'

Use real examples from school, work or projects. Arrive early, listen carefully and ask one or two questions at the end.

questions.text: What should you learn before an interview?
What is good to do at the end?

skills.title: Online Safety
skills.description: Keep your accounts and data safe.

lessons.title: Keeping Accounts Safe
lessons.content:
Use a different strong password for each account. A strong password is long and mixes words, numbers and symbols. A password manager can remember them for you.

Turn on two-step verification where you can, and never share your codes with anyone. Be careful with links in unexpected messages, because they may be scams.

questions.text: What makes a password strong?
options: Long with words, numbers and symbols

questions.text: What should you do with verification codes?

skills.title: Smartphone Tips
skills.description: Get more from the phone in your pocket.

lessons.title: Battery and Storage
lessons.content:
To save battery, lower the screen brightness, close apps you do not use and turn on battery saver when low.

If storage is full, delete unused apps, clear old downloads and back up photos to the cloud or a computer before deleting them from the phone.

questions.text: Which helps save battery?
What should you do before deleting photos?

skills.title: Spreadsheet Basics
skills.description: Cells, formulas and simple charts.

lessons.title: Cells and Formulas
lessons.content:
A spreadsheet is a grid of cells. Each cell has an address, like A1 (column A, row 1).

Formulas start with an equals sign. For example, =A1+B1 adds the values in A1 and B1, and =SUM(A1:A5) adds the five cells from A1 to A5.

questions.text: What does a formula start with?
What does =SUM(A1:A5) do?

skills.title: Workout Warm-Ups
skills.description: Prepare your body safely.

lessons.title: Warm Up Before Exercise
lessons.content:
A warm-up raises your heart rate and loosens your muscles so you are less likely to get hurt. Spend 5 to 10 minutes on light movement such as marching in place, arm circles and leg swings.

Save long static stretches, where you hold a position, for after your workout. Drink water and wear shoes that fit you well.

questions.text: How long should a warm-up take?
When are long static stretches best?

skills.title: Running for Beginners
skills.description: Build up distance without burning out.

lessons.title: Start with Walk-Run Intervals
lessons.content:
If you are new to running, mix walking and running. For example, run for one minute, walk for two minutes and repeat for 20 minutes.

Gradually increase the running time each week. Run at a pace where you can still talk, and rest at least one or two days a week to let your body recover.

questions.text: What is a good beginner approach?
What pace is good?
options: One where you can still talk

skills.title: Basketball Basics
skills.description: Dribbling, passing and shooting.

lessons.title: Dribbling and Shooting
lessons.content:
To dribble, use your fingertips, not your palm, and keep the ball low and close. Look up so you can see the court, not just the ball.

To shoot, bend your knees, keep your elbow under the ball, and follow through with your wrist, as if reaching into the basket.

questions.text: What part of the hand do you use to dribble?
What should you do while dribbling?

skills.title: Healthy Sleep
skills.description: Habits for deeper, better sleep.

lessons.title: Healthy Sleep Habits
lessons.content:
Most adults need around 7 to 9 hours of sleep. Go to bed and wake up at about the same time every day, even on weekends.

Keep your room dark and cool, and put screens away at least 30 minutes before bed. Avoid caffeine late in the afternoon.

questions.text: About how much sleep do most adults need?
What helps you sleep better?

skills.title: Stress Management
skills.description: Simple ways to feel calmer.

lessons.title: Breathing to Calm Down
lessons.content:
When you feel stressed, slow breathing can help. Try box breathing: breathe in for four counts, hold for four, breathe out for four and hold for four.

Repeat this several times. Regular movement, enough sleep and talking to someone you trust also help you handle stress.

questions.text: What is box breathing?
options: Breathe in, hold, out, hold, each for four counts
Holding your breath for a minute

questions.text: What else helps with stress?

skills.title: Basic First Aid
skills.description: Respond calmly to small injuries.

lessons.title: Cuts and Scrapes
lessons.content:
For a small cut, first wash your hands. Press a clean cloth on the cut to stop the bleeding, then rinse the cut with clean water.

Cover it with a clean bandage and change it daily. See a doctor if the bleeding does not stop, the cut is deep, or it becomes red, swollen or very painful.

questions.text: What should you do first for a small cut?
When should you see a doctor?
options: If bleeding does not stop or the cut is deep

skills.title: Goal Setting
skills.description: Turn wishes into clear plans.

lessons.title: Setting SMART Goals
lessons.content:
A goal works better when it is clear. SMART means Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

Instead of saying 'I want to read more', say 'I will read 10 pages every night for the next 30 days'. Then track your progress and celebrate small wins.

questions.text: What does the M in SMART stand for?
Which is the better goal?
options: Read 10 pages every night for 30 days

skills.title: Time Management
skills.description: Spend your time on what matters.

lessons.title: Prioritizing Tasks
lessons.content:
Write your tasks down, then sort them by importance and deadline. Do the most important tasks first, when your energy is highest.

Break big tasks into small steps, and avoid doing many things at once, because switching tasks wastes time.

questions.text: What should you do first?
Why break big tasks into steps?
options: They are easier to start and finish

skills.title: Building Good Habits
skills.description: Make small habits that last.

lessons.title: Start Small
lessons.content:
Habits form through repetition. Start with a very small action, like two minutes of reading or one glass of water each morning.

Attach the new habit to something you already do, such as after brushing your teeth. Track your streak, and if you miss a day, restart the next day instead of quitting.

questions.text: How should you start a new habit?
What if you miss a day?

skills.title: Travel Etiquette
skills.description: Respect local customs and people.

lessons.title: Respecting Local Customs
lessons.content:
Before you travel, learn a few basics about the place: common greetings, how to dress at religious sites, tipping habits and table manners.

Smile, say hello and thank you in the local language, and ask before taking photos of people. Being curious and polite goes a long way.

questions.text: What should you do before photographing a person?
Why learn local customs before traveling?

skills.title: Budget Travel Planning
skills.description: See more for less.

lessons.title: Planning a Trip Budget
lessons.content:
List your main costs: transport, places to stay, food, activities and a little extra for emergencies. Estimate each one before you book.

Travel outside peak season for lower prices, book transport early and keep track of what you spend each day.

questions.text: What should a trip budget include?
options: Transport, stay, food, activities and extra

questions.text: When are prices often lower?

skills.title: Packing Smart
skills.description: Pack light and still have what you need.

lessons.title: Pack Light
lessons.content:
Make a list before you pack. Choose clothes that can be mixed and matched, and wear your bulkiest items while traveling.

Put important items like documents, money and medicine in your carry-on bag, and leave some space for things you buy.

questions.text: Where should documents and money go?
What is a good packing idea?

skills.title: Chess Basics
skills.description: Rules, pieces and first strategies.

lessons.title: Learning the Rules of Chess
lessons.content:
Chess is played on an 8 x 8 board by two players. Each side starts with 16 pieces: one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights and eight pawns.

The goal is checkmate, which means the opponent's king is attacked and cannot escape. Bishops move diagonally, rooks move in straight lines and knights jump in an L shape.

questions.text: How do bishops move?
What is the goal of chess?

skills.title: Sudoku Basics
skills.description: Solve number puzzles with logic.

lessons.title: How Sudoku Works
lessons.content:
Sudoku is played on a 9 x 9 grid split into nine 3 x 3 boxes. Fill every row, column and box with the numbers 1 to 9, using each number once.

Start with rows, columns or boxes that already have many numbers, and find which number is missing. Use logic, not guessing.

questions.text: What numbers go in a Sudoku grid?
Can a number repeat in a row?

skills.title: Origami Basics
skills.description: Fold paper into simple shapes.

lessons.title: Basic Folds
lessons.content:
Origami is the art of folding paper. Two basic folds are the valley fold, where the paper folds toward you like a valley, and the mountain fold, where it folds away like a mountain.

Use a flat surface, make sharp creases with your fingernail and follow the steps in order.

questions.text: What is origami?
Which fold goes toward you like a valley?
